<!-- Generated from worked-example.Rmd.orig by precompute/precompile.R. Edit the .orig file, not this one. -->



This page takes five study designs through `powerape`, each in R and in
Stata. The teams are stylized; the questions are the ones a design
discussion has to answer:

* **Design A.** How many observations does a treatment effect worth acting
  on need?
* **Design B.** Can a moderation study find its interaction?
* **Design C.** What is last year's pilot worth for next year's design?
* **Design D.** How many firms does a firm-year panel need?
* **Design E.** What does instrumenting the treatment cost?

Each section states the setting, runs the calls that answer the question and
draws the lesson. The lessons are collected [at the
end](#the-five-designs-at-a-glance), with what a power analysis of this kind
should report. Choosing R or Stata on any tab switches the whole page.

The R code fixes its seeds, so its numbers reproduce exactly with the version
of the package named at the end. Stata draws different random numbers, so
its numbers agree with R's up to simulation error; the text quotes the two
side by side. In Stata, a single power call fits every simulated study with
Stata's own estimation command (`probit`, or `cfprobit` in Design E), and
the searches and sweeps use the faster Mata engine (see [Get started in
Stata](stata.html)).

## Claims, in one paragraph

Every design is priced for a claim about the confidence interval of the
effect, stated in probability points (Riesthuis, 2024). The
**minimum-effect claim** (`minimum`, the default) holds when the lower bound
of the interval exceeds the smallest effect size of interest (the SESOI), so
the effect is large enough to matter; **detection** (`detect`) holds when
the interval excludes zero; **equivalence** holds when the interval lies
within ±SESOI. Designs A, C and D are priced for the minimum-effect claim, B
and E for detection. Power is the share of simulated studies in which the
claim holds, and a required sample size is found by search and then
confirmed by a run four times as long.

## Design A: a treatment effect worth acting on

A team plans an archival study of a support program for firms. Without the
program, about 30 percent of firms survive the study window. Firm
characteristics explain a modest share of the latent variation in survival;
one standard-normal covariate with a signal of 0.10 stands in for them. The
program pays for itself if it raises survival by five percentage points, and
earlier evidence puts its effect near ten. The study should be able to
conclude that the program is worth its cost: a minimum-effect claim with a
SESOI of 0.05. This is the design question of the [home page](../index.html),
with the same seeds, taken all the way through here.

``` r
library(powerape)

dA <- ape_dgp(focal = pa_var("program", "binary", p = 0.5),
              covariates = list(pa_var("z", "normal")),
              baseline = 0.30, signal = 0.10)
dA <- set_ape(dA, target = 0.10)
dA
#> powerape DGP -- probit
#>   focal: program (binary, p = 0.50)
#>   covariates: z (normal, mean 0.00, sd 1.00) 
#>   baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.100
#>   true APE pinned at +0.1000 (beta_focal = 0.2857, implied P(Y=1 | focal=1) = 0.400)
```

</div>
<div class="tab-pane" id="a-world-stata" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="a-world-stata-tab">

```stata
powerape dgp a, focal(program, binary p(0.5)) covariates((z, normal))      ///
    baseline(0.30) signal(0.10)
powerape setape a, target(0.10)
```

### Power at 1,500 firms

<div class="lang-tabs">
<ul class="nav nav-tabs" role="tablist">
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link active" id="a-power-r-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#a-power-r" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="a-power-r" aria-selected="true" data-lang="r">R</button></li>

</ul>
<div class="tab-content">
<div class="tab-pane active" id="a-power-r" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="a-power-r-tab">


``` r
pA <- ape_power(dA, n = 1500, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
                nsim = 4000, seed = 501)
pA
#> powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
#>   probit, n = 1500, assumed true APE +0.1000, 90% CI (alpha = 0.05), nsim = 4000
#>   power = 0.663 (MCSE 0.007)
#>   outcomes: minimum 0.663 | detect-only 0.323 | inconclusive 0.014 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000
```

</div>
<div class="tab-pane" id="a-power-stata" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="a-power-stata-tab">

```stata
powerape power a, n(1500) claim(minimum) sesoi(0.05) nsim(4000) seed(501)
```

```{.stata-output}
powerape -- minimum-effect claim (CI lower bound > 0.050)
  probit, n = 1500, assumed true APE + 0.1000,     90% CI (alpha = .05), nsim = 4000
  fit: probit via engine(stata), effects(closed)
  power = 0.677 (MCSE 0.007)
  outcomes: minimum 0.677 | detect-only 0.312 | inconclusive 0.011 | equivalence 0.000 | failed 0.000
```

</div>
</div>
</div>

At 1,500 firms the minimum-effect claim holds in 66 percent
of the simulated studies (Stata: 68). The
outcome table shows where the others end: in
32 percent the interval excludes zero but
not 0.05. Those studies would find that the program works and still could
not say that it is worth its cost.


```{.stata-output}
  fit: Mata engine (Fisher scoring)
  search: 1 step(s); confirmed in 1 round(s) at nsim = 4000.
```

For 80 percent power the minimum-effect claim needs
2,091 firms and detection 663 (Stata:
2,084 and
663; the Stata code keeps its required n in
a local for the steps that follow). Concluding that the effect matters costs
3.2 times the sample of concluding that it
exists, so a study sized for detection would be about a third of the size
its authors need for the conclusion they want to draw.

### How much the guesses matter

The baseline rate and the signal are informed guesses. A sweep re-prices the
design at the required n over baselines from 0.20 to 0.40 and signals from 0
to 0.30.

<div class="lang-tabs">

``` r
                 grid_points = 3, nsim = 600, seed = 504, nmax = FALSE)
rA
```

Across the nine scenarios, power at 2,091 firms runs from
76 to 90 percent
(Stata, at its own 2,084:
73 to
92). The weakest scenario combines a
baseline of 0.40 with a signal of
0.00, and even there about three studies in four
reach the conclusion. The design does not hinge on getting the baseline or
the signal exactly right.

## Design B: a moderation study that could find its interaction

A second team expects the program to work better for family firms. That is a
claim about an interaction, and the effect size that states it is the
**average interaction effect (AIE)**: the difference, in probability points,
between the program's effect among family firms and its effect among the
others. The team states four numbers on the probability scale: survival of
0.30 for non-family firms without the program, a program effect of ten
points among them, a difference of three points between family and other
firms without the program, and an interaction of eight points. `set_aie()`
(in Stata, `powerape setaie`) turns them into a probit whose four cells
survive at 0.30, 0.40, 0.33 and 0.51. The design has no covariates. A second
world prices the same eight points as a plain main effect of the program.

<div class="lang-tabs">
<ul class="nav nav-tabs" role="tablist">
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link active" id="b-world-r-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#b-world-r" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="b-world-r" aria-selected="true" data-lang="r">R</button></li>
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link" id="b-world-stata-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#b-world-stata" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="b-world-stata" aria-selected="false" data-lang="stata">Stata</button></li>
</ul>
<div class="tab-content">
<div class="tab-pane active" id="b-world-r" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="b-world-r-tab">


``` r
dB <- set_ape(ape_dgp(focal = pa_var("program", "binary", p = 0.5),
                      baseline = 0.30), target = 0.08)

dBi <- ape_dgp(focal = pa_var("program", "binary", p = 0.5),
               moderator = pa_var("family", "binary", p = 0.5),
               baseline = 0.30)
dBi <- set_aie(dBi, target = 0.08, main_focal = 0.10, main_moderator = 0.03)
dBi
#> powerape DGP -- probit
#>   focal: program (binary, p = 0.50)
#>   moderator: family (binary, p = 0.50) (focal-by-moderator interaction included)
#>   covariates: none
#>   baseline P(Y=1 | reference) = 0.300, nuisance signal (latent pseudo-R2) = 0.000
#>   true AIE pinned at +0.0800 (beta_int = 0.1939)
#>   main APEs at reference: program +0.100 (beta = 0.2711), family +0.030 (beta = 0.0845)
```

</div>

Detecting the eight-point interaction with 80 percent power takes
4,514 firms; the same eight points as a main effect take
1,092 (Stata: 4,518 and
1,093). The interaction costs
4.1 times as much. The reason lies in the estimand: the
AIE is a difference of differences of four cell rates, each estimated from
about a quarter of the sample. Demanding a *meaningful* interaction, a
minimum-effect claim with a SESOI of its own, raises the requirement again
(see [Interaction effects](interaction-effects.html)).

The null side has a claim of its own. An equivalence claim lets a team show
that the program's effect differs between the two kinds of firm by less than
a margin it can defend, instead of reading a non-significant interaction
test as evidence that the effect is the same everywhere (see
[Equivalence](equivalence.html)).

## Design C: from last year's pilot to next year's design

A third team has a pilot of 900 firms from an earlier wave. The pilot-model
route builds the next study's world from a probit fitted to the pilot: it
resamples the pilot's covariate rows and keeps the fitted nuisance
coefficients, but not the program's coefficient. That one is solved again at
the design target, because the pilot's noisy estimate of the very effect
under study is the one thing a design should not inherit. The team targets
an effect of eight points and wants to show that it exceeds three.

The pilot is simulated here, so that the page runs anywhere. Stata cannot
draw R's random numbers, so the Stata tab reads the same 900 rows from a
file,
[design-c-pilot.csv](https://github.com/jespernwulff/powerape/blob/main/precompute/stata/design-c-pilot.csv),
and its probit reproduces R's coefficients.

<div class="lang-tabs">
<ul class="nav nav-tabs" role="tablist">
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link active" id="c-pilot-r-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#c-pilot-r" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="c-pilot-r" aria-selected="true" data-lang="r">R</button></li>
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link" id="c-pilot-stata-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#c-pilot-stata" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="c-pilot-stata" aria-selected="false" data-lang="stata">Stata</button></li>
</ul>
<div class="tab-content">
<div class="tab-pane active" id="c-pilot-r" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="c-pilot-r-tab">


``` r
set.seed(31)
z        <- rnorm(900)
program  <- rbinom(900, 1, 0.5)
survived <- rbinom(900, 1, pnorm(-0.55 + 0.35 * program + 0.45 * z))
pilot    <- data.frame(survived, program, z)

fit <- glm(survived ~ program + z, family = binomial("probit"), data = pilot)
coef(summary(fit))
#>               Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -0.5771775 0.06528506 -8.840882 9.496624e-19
#> program      0.3392172 0.08947999  3.790984 1.500515e-04
#> z            0.4577795 0.04796170  9.544688 1.365184e-21
```

</div>
<div class="tab-pane" id="c-pilot-stata" role="tabpanel" aria-labelledby="c-pilot-stata-tab">


The pilot implies a baseline of 0.303, and at that
baseline the design needs 1,986 firms (Stata:
1,985). If the next study will run in a harsher
environment, with a baseline of 0.25 instead, one changed argument
re-prices the whole design: 1,819 firms (Stata:
1,822). Outcomes near a rate of 0.25 are
slightly less noisy than near 0.30, so the same eight points are a little
easier to establish.

Two cautions. This is prospective design for the next study, not "observed
power" for the pilot, which remains a fallacy (Hoenig & Heisey, 2001). And a
world built from a pilot inherits the pilot's sampling noise: with fewer than
500 pilot rows, `powerape` warns that the design's context is itself an
estimate.

## Design D: a firm-year panel, priced in firms

A fourth team plans a panel: firms observed over four annual waves, an
adoption event that is constant within the window, and the outcome,
baseline and covariate signal of Design A. The analysis will be a correlated
random effects (CRE) probit with Mundlak (1978) means and firm-clustered
standard errors, so the design is simulated for that estimator. Two panel
quantities must be stated: **rho**, the share of the unexplained latent
variation that is stable within firms (0.30, the rho of `xtprobit`), and the
share of that stable part that tracks the firms' observed averages (one
half). Sample sizes now count firms. The [Panel designs](panel-designs.html)
workflow describes the route in detail.

### Panel rows are not independent firms

Three hundred firms over four waves are 1,200 firm-years. The second world
draws the same 1,200 rows as independent firms.

The panel of 300 firms reaches 56 percent power for the
minimum-effect claim, the 1,200 independent firms 59 percent,
3 points more (Stata:
55 and
58 percent, from
4,000 replications each; R uses
20,000 to pin down a gap this small, but under `probit` each
simulated panel costs Stata many times what it costs R's engine). Two common
intuitions both fail
here. Panel rows are not independent firms: when firms differ in unobserved
ways, a firm's repeated rows carry less information than as many new firms
would. Nor are they nearly redundant, as the design effects of
cluster-randomized trials would suggest: in this world half of the stable
firm effect tracks the firms' observed averages, and the Mundlak means absorb
that part instead of wasting it. Even with no firm heterogeneity at all, the
CRE estimator would trail a cross-section of the same size, because holding
the firm means fixed spends about 1/T of the identifying variation: a
premium worth paying, since rho is never known to be zero.

Eighty percent power takes 572 firms, or
2,288 firm-years (Stata: 573
firms). As rho moves from 0.10 to 0.50, power at 300 firms falls from
59 to 52 percent
(Stata: 59 to
51). Rho, not the number of rows, is the
quantity a reviewer should probe: once it is non-trivial, firms rather than
rows buy power, and what a panel's waves are worth is a property of the
design that the simulation computes.

### Attrition

Firms drop out. The next two worlds keep each firm from one wave to the next
with probability 0.85 or 0.70, and the estimator becomes the CRE probit for
unbalanced panels of Wooldridge (2019): Mundlak means over the waves a firm
is observed, and indicators for the number of those waves.

<div class="lang-tabs">
<ul class="nav nav-tabs" role="tablist">
<li class="nav-item" role="presentation"><button class="nav-link active" id="d-attrition-r-tab" data-bs-toggle="tab" data-bs-target="#d-attrition-r" type="button" role="tab" aria-controls="d-attrition-r" aria-selected="true" data-lang="r">R</button></li>

``` r
retained <- function(r) {
  d <- ape_dgp_panel(focal = pa_var("adopt", "binary", p = 0.5, icc = 1),
                     covariates = list(pa_var("size", "normal", icc = 0.6)),
                     n_periods = 4, retention = r, rho = 0.30,
                     cre_share = 0.50, baseline = 0.30, signal = 0.10,
                     n_int = 4e4)
  set_ape(d, target = 0.10)
}
dD85 <- retained(0.85)
dD70 <- retained(0.70)
```


``` r
p85 <- ape_power(dD85, n = 300, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
                 nsim = 10000, seed = 71)
p70 <- ape_power(dD70, n = 300, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
                 nsim = 10000, seed = 71)
n85 <- ape_n(dD85, power = 0.80, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
             nsim = 800, seed = 72)
n70 <- ape_n(dD70, power = 0.80, claim = "minimum", sesoi = 0.05,
             nsim = 800, seed = 72)
data.frame(retention  = c(1, 0.85, 0.70),
           waves      = round(c(4, dD85$expected_T, dD70$expected_T), 2),
           power_300  = round(c(pD$power, p85$power, p70$power), 3),
           firms      = c(nD$n, n85$n, n70$n),
           firm_years = round(c(4 * nD$n, n85$n * dD85$expected_T,
                                n70$n * dD70$expected_T)))
#>   retention waves power_300 firms firm_years
#> 1      1.00  4.00     0.563   572       2288
#> 2      0.85  3.19     0.499   699       2227
#> 3      0.70  2.53     0.435   843       2135
```

699 and 843 firms (Stata:
49 and
42 percent from
2,000 replications each;
701 and 849
firms). In firm-years the three requirements are close, about
2,290, 2,230
and 2,140: what attrition removes is
rows per firm, and recruitment has to make them up. A proposal can budget
for its expected retention instead of hoping for it.

## Design E: what instrumenting a treatment costs

A fifth team studies a treatment that firms choose for themselves,
participation in a training program, with a subsidy offer as the instrument.
The analysis will be a control-function probit (Wooldridge, 2015): a
first-stage probit of participation on the instrument, whose generalized
residual enters the outcome probit. This is the estimator of Stata's
`cfprobit`, and in the Stata tab `cfprobit` fits every simulated study of a
single power call. Two quantities are new: the correlation between the
errors of the two equations, which is why the treatment must be instrumented
at all (`endogeneity`, here 0.4), and the strength of the first stage, the
instrument's share of the latent variation in participation (`iv_strength`,
here 0.2). A second world is the same design with an exogenous treatment. The
[IV designs](iv-designs.html) workflow describes the route in detail.

At 1,200 observations the exogenous design detects the ten-point APE with
96 percent power, the instrumented design with
22 percent (Stata: 96
and 22). Nothing about the effect changed,
only the share of the variation the estimator is allowed to use. The control
function identifies the effect mainly from the instrumented share, so its
standard error exceeds the exogenous one by roughly the square root of
1/`iv_strength`, about 2.2 here, and the endogeneity assumed in this world
pushes the surcharge higher still.

Holding the effect fixed, power at 1,200 observations runs from
12 to 32 percent
as the instrument's share moves from 0.10 to 0.30 (Stata:
14 to
32): first-stage strength is the
elicitation that matters most. A moderated version in the spirit of Design
B, a six-point AIE between public and private firms with an instrument share
of 0.25, reaches only 10 percent power at 2,000
observations (Stata: 10), because it
pays both surcharges at once. A study sized for a plain probit that turns to
instruments at review time has not gained a robustness check; it has lost
the study. Budget for the estimator the analysis will report: a few minutes
of simulation show the cost before the data are collected.

## The five designs at a glance

| Design | Question | Required n, R | Required n, Stata | Lesson |
|:--|:----------|:------|:------|:--------------|
| A | How many firms for an effect worth acting on? | 2,091 vs. 663 | 2,084 vs. 663 | A meaningful conclusion costs about three times the sample of mere detection. |
| B | Can the moderation study find its interaction? | 4,514 vs. 1,092 | 4,518 vs. 1,093 | The same eight points cost about four times as much as an interaction as they do as a main effect. |
| C | What is last year's pilot worth? | 1,986 vs. 1,819 | 1,985 vs. 1,822 | The pilot contributes its world, never its effect; one changed argument re-prices the design. |
| D | How many firms for a firm-year panel? | 572; 699 and 843 | 573; 701 and 849 | Sample size counts firms, rho is the elicitation that matters, and attrition costs firms, not firm-years. |
| E | What does instrumenting the treatment cost? | 6,813 vs. 699 | 6,750 vs. 732 | Instrumenting multiplies the requirement almost tenfold; budget for the estimator the analysis will report. |

Required sample sizes for 80 percent power, for each design's own claim: the
minimum-effect claim in A, C and D, detection in B and E. A: minimum effect
vs. detection. B: the AIE vs. the same effect as a main effect. C: the
pilot's baseline vs. a baseline of 0.25. D: firms in the balanced panel, then
with retention of 0.85 and 0.70. E: the control function vs. an exogenous
treatment. Each is a seeded estimate accepted by the confirmation run; other
seeds move it by a few percent without changing any comparison above.

## What to report

A design paragraph in a proposal or a preregistration should let a reader
re-run the analysis and judge its assumptions. It reports:

* the estimand and its units: the APE or the AIE, in probability points,
  with the model and link;
* the SESOI, with its substantive justification;
* the claim, its error rate and the interval level it implies, and how the
  error rate was chosen;
* the planning value, the effect at which power was computed, and why;
* the assumed world and its source: baseline rate, covariates and their
  dependence, nuisance signal, panel or first-stage quantities where they
  apply; parametric guesses, pilot rows or a pilot model;
* that the target is feasible in that world;
* power at the chosen n with its Monte Carlo standard error, and the full
  outcome table;
* the robustness range: what was swept, the range of power and the worst
  case, and n_max where relevant;
* the software and its version, the seed and the number of replications.

`power_statement()` (in Stata, `powerape statement`) writes the estimand,
world, claim and power items as a paragraph; the feasibility check, the
robustness range and the seeds come from the same session. For Design A at
its required n:

## Notes on reproducibility

* The R output on this page comes from `powerape`
  1.11.3, the Stata output from the Stata command
  0.1.2 (StataNow 19.5). Every call shows its seed and its number
  of replications, so with the same versions the R numbers reproduce
  exactly.
* R and Stata draw different random numbers, so their numbers agree up to
  simulation error, not digit for digit.
* A required sample size is confirmed by a run with four times the search's
  replications (16,000 in Design E's instrumented search), and the search
  never trims n after an overshoot. A required n therefore inherits the noise
  of the power estimates near the target, and the two languages can land a
  few percent apart: for Design E's exogenous comparison, R stops at
  699 and Stata at 732, where
  its confirmation run found a power of
  .82.
* In Stata, the single power calls fit every simulated study with Stata's own
  commands: `probit` (with `vce(cluster)` on the panel route) and `cfprobit`
  on the IV route. That is slower: the
  4,000 simulated panels of Design D's first
  power call took 14 minutes this way, on a machine that
  was busy with other jobs. The searches and
  sweeps use the Mata engine, which follows the R package's conventions and
  is 10 to 30 times faster; the two engines agree up to simulation error
  (see [How powerape is validated](validation.html)).
* The Stata code uses the R code's numbers of replications throughout, except
  in Design D's single power calls: 4,000
  and 2,000 replications where R uses
  20,000 and 10,000: under `probit` each
  simulated panel costs Stata many times what it costs R's engine, so the
  Stata run keeps these counts down.
* The Stata runs behind this page are in the package's repository, in
  [precompute/stata](https://github.com/jespernwulff/powerape/tree/main/precompute/stata)
  (`worked-example-a.do` to `worked-example-e.do`).
